text.title: Competitive Analysis (UX) Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules every Competitive Analysis (UX) application MUST enforce, plus a skip-this-methodology fallback. These are HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them. Structured procedure for examining competitor products across predefined criteria and converting observations into prioritized design recommendations.

rule.statement: The competitor set MUST include 3-5 direct + 2-3 indirect + 1-2 aspirational competitors. Single-bucket analyses are rejected. Select 3-5 direct competitors, 2-3 indirect competitors, and 1-2 aspirational examples. Cap total at 8 to maintain analysis depth.
rule.rationale: Direct competitors set the baseline; indirect reveal alternative approaches; aspirational reveal best-in-class targets. More than 8 competitors degrades analysis depth — breadth replaces insight. Aspirational examples from adjacent industries expose solutions that direct competitors have not discovered.

rule.statement: Evaluation criteria MUST be declared before any competitor is examined. Post-hoc criterion addition is rejected. Establish evaluation criteria before examining any competitor product — criteria derived after examination are biased toward what was observed.
rule.rationale: Post-hoc criteria become rationalisation; pre-declaration keeps the analysis honest. Post-hoc criteria selection produces confirmation bias — analysts unconsciously weight criteria where their preferred design performs well. Pre-defined criteria are neutral.

rule.statement: Every finding MUST be classified Must | Should | Could | Avoid. Loose findings without classification are rejected. Categorize every recommendation into Must Have (table stakes), Should Have (competitive parity), Could Differentiate (opportunity), or Avoid (observed failure mode). Use a four-tier recommendation structure in every competitive analysis report: Must Have (table stakes), Should Have (parity), Could Differentiate (opportunity), Avoid (observed failure mode).
rule.rationale: Without MSCW the analysis is documentation, not a decision artefact. Flat recommendation lists produce debate. Four-tier categorization produces a prioritization decision: Must Have items are blockers; Avoid items are negative signals; differentiation opportunities are the most valuable output. Without tiers, all recommendations appear equal and teams debate which to implement first. Tiers pre-empt the debate by making priority explicit from the analysis.

rule.statement: Each competitor profile MUST be based on first-hand product use, not marketing copy. Profiles assembled from websites only are rejected. Create real accounts and complete full user flows rather than reviewing screenshots or marketing pages.
rule.rationale: Marketing copy hides the actual UX; first-hand use surfaces the real friction. Screenshots reveal visual design only. Friction, error states, loading behavior, and onboarding quality are only visible through direct use. Surface-level review misses the most actionable findings.

rule.statement: Each finding MUST cite a screenshot or session-recording reference. Uncited claims are rejected.
rule.rationale: Citations make the analysis falsifiable; uncited claims are opinion.

rule.statement: Use the same documentation structure for every competitor — annotated screenshots, flow steps, strengths, weaknesses, and opportunities. Inconsistent documentation prevents comparison.
rule.rationale: Inconsistent notes cannot be compared across competitors. A structured template forces coverage of the same criteria for all products.

rule.statement: After documenting all competitors, identify: what everyone does (baseline expectation), what nobody does (opportunity gap), what top performers do distinctively (best practice), and what common problems exist (anti-patterns to avoid).
rule.rationale: Pattern analysis across competitors is where individual observations become strategic insight. Analyzing one competitor at a time produces a list of features, not a competitive landscape.

rule.statement: If any Applies-If precondition fails OR any Skip-If condition triggers, do NOT apply this methodology. Emit a skip-record naming the failed precondition / triggered skip, and route the task to the correct methodology (or none).
rule.rationale: Methodology hygiene: mis-application produces worse artefacts than no methodology because downstream consumers trust the schema; the skip-record makes non-application traceable.
